title: Jnaneshwar
hook: the Gita, carried out of Sanskrit and into the language of the street

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jnaneshwar: the outcast boy at Paithan who put his hand on a buffalo's head, and the buffalo recited the Veda. Whose voice did you actually listen to? Day nine hundred fourteen.

A temple in a small town by a river. A young man sits near a stone pillar and talks, verse by verse, through the Bhagavad Gita. Not in Sanskrit, the language of the priests. In Marathi, the language of the farmers, the potters, the women at the well, the people sitting in front of him. Next to him, someone is writing every word down. What comes out of those talks is a book that people in Maharashtra still read aloud together. Today, Jnaneshwar's Gita.
screen: `A TEMPLE BY A RIVER.` → `THE GITA, IN MARATHI.` → `SOMEONE WRITES IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Tradition says this happened at Nevasa, and that the man writing was Sachchidananda, who took down Jnaneshwar's words as he spoke. The book is called the Jnaneshwari, after him, and it isn't a translation in the usual sense. It walks through the Gita verse by verse and opens each one up, with pictures from ordinary life. A tortoise drawing in its limbs. A lamp burning where no wind reaches. Images the Gita gives in a line, he lingers over at length. Here's the part to notice. Remember Paithan, where scholars laughed at outcast children. Now one of those children takes a teaching most people met in Sanskrit, a language few of his listeners had studied, and opens it in the everyday language, for anyone who can listen. In one passage, he makes a promise about his Marathi: he will make his words so sweet they would win a wager against nectar. That's not a modest claim. It's a bet that the language of the street can carry the deepest things. And then the humility. Throughout the book, Jnaneshwar keeps handing the credit to his teacher, Nivritti, who is also his older brother. He speaks of himself as a child, and of everything good in the book as his teacher's grace. So you have a young man making the boldest claim about language, and the smallest claim about himself, in the same book. People in the Varkari tradition read the Jnaneshwari in groups, and walk with it on pilgrimage. The same pages that were spoken by a pillar are still spoken out loud.
screen: `SPOKEN AT NEVASA, WRITTEN DOWN.` · `THE GITA OPENED IN MARATHI.` · `SWEETER THAN NECTAR.` · `ALL CREDIT TO HIS BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your breath find its own pace. Think of one teaching, from any source, that only made sense to you once someone put it in plain words. A parent. A teacher. A friend at a kitchen table. Bring their voice to mind, the exact way they said it. Let gratitude for them be the thing you hold. If you pray, you can thank God for them, in words you already use. If not, simply say their name to yourself, once. The bell holds the time.
Jnaneshwar. The Marathi saint whose Jnaneshwari opened the Bhagavad Gita, verse by verse, in the language people spoke at home.
Your line: sweeter than nectar. Today, explain one thing you know in the plainest words you can, to someone who's been left out of it. Day nine hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Varkari devotees read the Jnaneshwari aloud in groups, at home and in temples, and many read it along the way on the pilgrimage to Pandharpur.

notes: Editor pass: 'turns over for a page' softened (length claim); 'the very teaching they guarded' changed to 'a teaching kept in Sanskrit' so the Paithan scholars are not cast as a foil.

Audit: cut a teach sentence that repeated the hook's Sanskrit-versus-Marathi point; trapdoor 'the guarded language' changed (implied Brahmin gatekeeping as a foil); howItsDone no longer says the book itself is carried on the wari (the palkhi carries his padukas).
All paraphrase. The 'win a wager against nectar' promise is from the opening of chapter 6 (around ovi 14); confirm reference and paraphrase.
Nevasa and Sachchidananda as scribe: from the colophon of the Jnaneshwari as tradition reads it; attributed to 'tradition says'. Confirm.
The common statements of his age and the date of composition are deliberately omitted under the claims rule.
Images (the tortoise, Gita 2.58; the lamp in a windless place, Gita 6.19) are from the Gita, which the Jnaneshwari expands; 'he turns over for a page' is a loose description; confirm.
Sanskrit framed as 'the language of the learned'; confirm.
